blocks.text: [Name], this report is about one thing: what happens in the room when you present, and how to make more of it happen on purpose.

You may never have chosen to present. You might be the finance director walking the board through the numbers, the consultant pitching every few weeks, the team leader briefing on Monday morning. You do it well enough. This report is about getting from good enough to better than most. In thirty years of coaching I have found that the distance is shorter than most people think.

You answered sixty questions about how you prepare and how you present. This report turns your answers into a picture of where you are strong, where you have most to gain, and what to work on first. It takes about forty minutes to read properly. Read it with your next presentation in mind.
Every presentation that works does three things.

blocks.label: Fit
blocks.text: It is built for the people in the room. You know who is in the room, what they already believe, what they need to hear, and what they should do afterwards. Fit happens before you open the slide software.

blocks.label: Focus
blocks.text: It makes one argument, clearly. You have decided what the point is, cut what does not serve it, and given the audience a structure they can follow and remember.

blocks.label: Flair
blocks.text: It sticks in their minds. Flair has two parts. The message: language, stories and examples that cannot be forgotten. The delivery: voice, body and presence that carry the message to every person listening.

The order matters. Fit comes first because everything else depends on it. Focus gives Flair something solid to stand on. Dynamic delivery of a disorganised message leaves the audience entertained but unsure what they have heard.

Each of the four dimensions has a score out of 100. A score of 60 or above is a capital F: a strength you can rely on, and still develop. A score below 60 is a small f: an area where small changes and practice will pay back fastest. Your three letters, one each for Fit, Focus and Flair, give your profile: [code], [profile name].

Under the four dimensions sit fifteen subscales. Each is a specific habit, such as defining the objective or using your voice with skill. The report ranks all fifteen, from the one with the most to gain to your strongest suit. The two at the top of that list are your development priorities. Each gets a full page: what the score means, a note written for you, a principle to hold on to, and five things to practise.
Three things to keep in mind.

items: These are your own ratings of yourself, so they show how you see your presenting today.
A score describes a habit, and habits change with practice.
And the most useful number in the report is the lowest one, because that is where a small change shows up as a big difference quickly.

blocks.text: Read your profile first, then your two priorities. Leave the detail in the subscales for a second sitting.

Then pick your next real presentation, however small, and apply the one thing your profile suggests. A Monday briefing will do. After it, ask one question: what difference did the change make to me, and my audience? If the answer is clear, it worked.

The last page sets out a 90-day plan built on your two priorities. Each subscale page names the chapter of the accompanying book, Fit, Focus and Flair that goes deeper, and the workbook exercise to practise it. If your priorities sit in building the story, StoryMachine will help you build your next one. Your link is on the last page.

FFF.name: The Complete Presenter
FFF.tag: High Fit, high Focus, high Flair
says: You are strong in all three areas. You prepare with the audience in mind, you say what needs saying without overloading people, and you present in a way that is memorable. That combination is rarer than it sounds.
The risk at this level is repetition. A strong approach, run without variation, slowly becomes a habit. And habits, however effective, stop you noticing what could be better.

The most useful question to sit with is what you are avoiding. You probably have a situation you quietly sidestep: the difficult room, the hostile audience, the brief that asks them to say something people do not want to hear. That is where your next level of skill gets built.
[[PERSONAL]]
questions: When did you last present in a situation that unsettled you? What did you learn from it?
Is there a type of audience or occasion you tend to avoid? What stops you from seeking it out?
If a colleague described your presenting style in three words, what would they be? Are you comfortable with that answer?
What would presenting one level above where you are now look and feel like?
FFF.tryThis: Seek out a presenting situation you find difficult and go towards it on purpose. Step outside your comfort zone deliberately.

FFf.name: The Solid Presenter
FFf.tag: High Fit, high Focus, developing Flair
says: Your presentations are well prepared and well targeted. You think about the audience, you structure clearly, and you do not waste people's time. Colleagues regard you as reliable.

Your opportunity is to make your messages unforgettable. People leave your presentations having understood the point. Two weeks later, they remember that you said something sensible. The specifics are harder to recall.

This is a preparation habit, and it can be learned. You have built a strong structure, and you stay inside it. The next step is to give yourself permission to step outside it: one story told well, one sharp and honest observation, one moment of real connection, one headline that sticks in people's minds and matches what is at stake for the people in the room. These are what move a message into long-term memory.
[[PERSONAL]]
questions: Think about your last presentation. Which one moment would you most like the audience to remember? Did you plan it, or leave it to chance?
When did you last share a personal story or real example in a presentation? What stopped you doing it more often?
What one thing could you add to your next presentation to make it more human and less formal?
Who is a presenter you admire? What do they do that you do not yet allow yourself to do?
FFf.tryThis: Before your next presentation, decide on the one moment you want the audience to talk about afterwards. Plan it on purpose.

FfF.name: The Compelling Presenter
FfF.tag: High Fit, developing Focus, high Flair
says: You are interesting to listen to. You understand your audience, you bring energy and personality, and people pay attention when you speak. In many meetings, you are the most engaging presenter.

Your opportunity is clarity and brevity. Your audiences enjoy the experience of listening to you talk. They are sometimes less certain what you wanted them to take away. The presentation is rich, and at times it is hard to follow.

The instinct behind this is generosity. You give people a lot: more context, more examples, more angles than they need. The audience can only carry so much out of the room. If you do not decide what the single most important thing is, they will decide for themselves, and they may choose something you never intended.
[[PERSONAL]]
questions: Before your last presentation, did you write down in one sentence what you needed the audience to believe or do at the end?
Which parts of your presentations do audiences respond to most strongly? Do those parts carry the central argument?
When you edit a presentation, is your instinct to add or to cut? What would happen if you reversed it?
If you had to give your last presentation in half the time, what would you keep?
FfF.tryThis: Write your conclusion before anything else. If you cannot say in one sentence what you want the audience to do or believe at the end, you are not ready to build the presentation yet.

Fff.name: The Knowledgeable Presenter
Fff.tag: High Fit, developing Focus, developing Flair
says: You care about getting it right for the audience. You do the preparation and you take the work seriously. Those things matter and they show.

Your opportunity is in adding impact to your message. There is a tendency to present more than people need, in a form that is harder to follow than the content requires. The audience senses the effort. They do not always sense a clear, central point.

The common trap here is to mistake thoroughness for quality. Covering everything often stops a presentation from being good. The foundation is there: you already think about the audience. The next step is discipline. Decide what they most need to hear, remove everything that does not serve it, and find one way to make that message stick.
[[PERSONAL]]
questions: After your last presentation, what do you think the audience remembered? Have you asked them? Is that what you intended?
How do you decide what to include and what to leave out? Is there a principle behind it, or does most material stay in by default?
What would it feel like to present in two-thirds of your usual time? What would you have to let go of?
When did a presentation of yours surprise or move an audience? What was different about it?
Fff.tryThis: For your next presentation, set a time limit of two-thirds of what you would normally take. Build to that limit and notice what survives the cut. Start with the detail. Ask yourself what you could take out, and prompt the audience to ask questions, if they want more.

fFF.name: The Natural Presenter
fFF.tag: Developing Fit, high Focus, high Flair
says: You are good at this. You are clear and structured, and you have the kind of presence that makes people want to listen. The delivery is strong and the material is well shaped.
Your opportunity is subtle. Your presentations tend to start from your world. The best ones almost always start from the audience's.

This often goes unnoticed because the delivery carries it. Over time, people who see you present regularly may sense that your presentations feel familiar: the same energy, the same structure, the same perspective. Impressive, and built a little less around them than it could be. Familiarity is no substitute for preparation.
[[PERSONAL]]
questions: Before your last presentation, did you speak to anyone in the audience to find out what they wanted from it?
Think of a presentation that landed less well than you expected. What did you assume about the audience that turned out to be wrong?
Is there one question you could ask before any presentation that would reliably improve how well it connects?
How does an audience know when a presentation was built on real insight about them? What can you learn from that?
fFF.tryThis: Before you next present to an audience you think you know, ask one or two people what they most hope to take away. Then build the presentation around their answer.

fFf.name: The Clear Presenter
fFf.tag: Developing Fit, high Focus, developing Flair
says: Your strength is clarity. You make your point, you keep to time, and your presentations have a logical shape that is easy to follow. In a world full of people who waffle, that is useful.

Your opportunity is connection and impact. Your presentations are easy to understand and harder to remember. At times they feel like well-organised information downloaded for an audience to make sense of on their own.

Two things will close that gap. The first is your empathy (how they think and how they feel) for the audience: you structure well, often around your material, and the next step is to structure around what this audience needs from it today. The second is human interest: a real story, a concrete example, something that makes abstract content feel real. Both are additions to a preparation process that already works.
[[PERSONAL]]
questions: When you prepare, at what point do you think about the specific people who will be in the room?
What was the last story or real example you used in a presentation? How did the audience react? What stops you from using more?
If someone at your last presentation described it to a colleague, what would they say?
What would make a presentation of yours feel personal to the audience?
fFf.tryThis: Find one real example or story that shows your main point and build it into your next presentation. Two minutes of something concrete and human will do more than ten minutes of well-structured logic.

ffF.name: The Engaging Presenter
ffF.tag: Developing Fit, developing Focus, high Flair
says: People enjoy your presentations. You have energy, personality and the ability to make an audience feel something. These are the hardest qualities to teach, and you have them already.

Your opportunity sits between enjoyment and impact. Audiences leave feeling good about the experience. They are less clear about what you needed them to do or think. Your personality and performance are doing most of the work.

Two things will make a big difference. The first is to know and show you care about your audience before you prepare, as well as before you walk in. The second is structure: one clear argument, with a beginning that sets up a question, a middle that answers it, and an end that tells people what to do next. Your flair is an asset. Right now it carries weight that structure should share.
[[PERSONAL]]
questions: After a presentation that went well, how much of the success came from preparation and how much from delivery on the day?
When did you last research an audience before presenting to them? What difference did it make?
What was the central argument of your last presentation, in one sentence?
What would a presentation of yours look like if you spent as long on structure as you spend on delivery?
ffF.tryThis: Before your next presentation, write down the one-sentence argument you are making. Make it a claim someone could disagree with. Then check that every part of the presentation serves it.

fff.name: The Developing Presenter
fff.tag: Developing Fit, developing Focus, developing Flair
says: You were honest with yourself when you answered these questions. That matters more than the scores. The people who answer truthfully are the ones who improve fastest.
Your results show room to grow in all three areas. Taken all at once that can feel like a lot. Taken in the right order, it is manageable.

Start with Fit, because everything else depends on it. A presentation that begins from a clear understanding of what the audience needs has the wind behind it from the start. Then work on Focus: decide the one thing you most need them to take away and cut everything that does not serve it. Flair comes last, because it needs a structure to sit on.
[[PERSONAL]]
questions: Think of a presentation that went less well than you hoped. Where did it start to go wrong: the audience preparation, the structure, or the delivery?
What is one thing about the way you prepare that you know is holding you back? What would it take to change it?
Who presents in a way you admire? What do they do that you do not yet do?
If you could change one thing before your next presentation, which would give you the most return?
fff.tryThis: For your next presentation, answer three questions in writing before you prepare anything else. Who exactly is in the room? What do they most need to hear? What do you want them to do when you finish? Those answers are your brief.

Builds empathy for the audience.name: Builds empathy for the audience
Builds empathy for the audience.measures: How well you understand the people in the meeting before you prepare: what they know, what they believe, how they feel about your subject, and what they need from you. It covers the research you do and how far you change a presentation for each audience.

score.high: You start with people. You find out who is in the room and you shape the presentation around them. Audiences feel that, even when they cannot name it.
score.low: Your opportunity is to start with people. You probably know your material well and prepare it with care. The next step is to spend the first part of your preparation on the audience: how they think and how they feel.

Builds empathy for the audience.matters: An audience decides in the first few minutes whether you understand their world. If you do, they lean in and give you the benefit of the doubt. If you do not, they listen politely and change nothing. Empathy is the cheapest preparation you can do, and it raises the value of everything else.

high: Find out what the audience believes about your subject today and what you want them to believe at the end. Write down the gap. That gap is your presentation.
List what success means to the key people in the room: targets, recognition, reputation, security, the avoidance of harm. Show each of them how your proposal moves theirs forward.
If the gap between what they believe and what you need is too wide for one meeting, plan two or three. Influencing is the art of patience.
Fit your approach to the audience in front of you on the day. If the mood in the room has changed, change your opening.
Work out what the most sceptical person in the room has heard before. If they have sat through eleven "all hands" meetings, open with something new.
low: Before you prepare anything, write down five things you know about this audience. Where you cannot complete the list, you have found your research.
Ask two or three of the most influential people who will be there for the three things they most want from the presentation. They will also tell you what they do not want. Build from their answers.
Write a short email as if you were one of them, to a friend, about the problem you are there to solve. If it is hard to write, you do not yet know them well enough.
Before you prepare, ask someone who knows the audience three questions: what will interest them, what will not, and what would make a good impression on them?
Start kind and respectful. It is safer to give your status away than to take theirs. Earn your place in the first two minutes.

practise.high: Find out what the audience believes about your subject today and what you want them to believe at the end. Write down the gap. That gap is your presentation.
practise.low: Before you prepare anything, write down five things you know about this audience. Where you cannot complete the list, you have found your research.

note.text: Understand the people in the audience. Assume the very best and highest ambitions, values and principles for them.

Builds empathy for the audience.deeper: Chapter Two. Workbook Tool 1: Audience Analysis.

online.title: The most important thing that trumps all when presenting

Understands themselves as a speaker.name: Understands themselves as a speaker
Understands themselves as a speaker.measures: How well you know your own strengths and habits as a presenter, how you seek and use feedback, and how you think about the way this audience will see you and your point of view.

score.high: You know what you do well and what you are working on. You ask for feedback and you use it. That habit keeps you improving.
score.low: You have an opportunity to see yourself as the audience sees you. You may never have watched yourself present. A little honest feedback will show you where your effort pays back fastest.

Understands themselves as a speaker.matters: The audience forms a view of you before they form a view of your argument. If you know how you come across, and what this audience may assume about you, you can work with it. Knowing your own biases about the subject also helps you answer the hard question when it comes.

high: Ask for feedback on one specific thing at your next presentation: your opening, your pace, or how you handle questions.
Before you prepare, write down what this audience may assume about you: your role, your seniority, your department. Decide how you will use the first two minutes to work with it.
Keep self-deprecating humour for rooms where you are the most senior person. Anywhere else, the audience may believe you.
Find the version of you that works best in the room: your own character, expanded a little. Have an argument, have an opinion, and say it as yourself.
Ask how this audience sees your status: your role, your reputation, your track record. Decide whether to raise it or lower it in your opening.
low: Record yourself rehearsing for five minutes and watch it back. Write down one thing that works and one thing to change.
Ask a trusted colleague to watch your next presentation and tell you the one thing they would change. Ask a precise question and you will get a precise answer.
Know your type. If you are an introvert, remember to speak after all that thinking. If you are an extrovert, remember to think before you speak.
Write down three words a colleague would use to describe you as a presenter. Ask one colleague for their three words, and compare.
Show your own view. Add one opinion of your own to your next presentation, and say why you hold it.

practise.high: Ask for feedback on one specific thing at your next presentation: your opening, your pace, or how you handle questions.
practise.low: Record yourself rehearsing for five minutes and watch it back. Write down one thing that works and one thing to change.

note.text: Hide behind the content and most of the interest for the audience is gone.

Understands themselves as a speaker.deeper: Chapter Four, Section Two. Workbook Tool 11: The Feedback Request.

online.title: How to get over Impostor Syndrome when you are presenting

Understands their subject.name: Understands their subject
Understands their subject.measures: How well you know the limits of your own knowledge, how current your evidence is, and what you do to close the gaps before you present.

score.high: You check your evidence and you know where your knowledge runs out. That gives you confidence under questions.
score.low: Your opportunity is to find the gaps before the audience does. A short check of your evidence before each presentation will lift your credibility quickly.

Understands their subject.matters: Gaps in knowledge show up under questions. A stale figure or an old example tells the audience you have stopped paying attention. Being honest about what you do not know builds more trust than covering it up.

high: Refresh one example in a presentation you give often. Replace it with something from the last three months.
Give the big idea, then come down quickly to a concrete example the audience can use. Experts lose people when they stay at either level too long.
Ask who each piece of detail is for. Keep what this audience needs to act, and put the rest in a note they can read afterwards.
Keep a running file of fresh facts and stories for your subject, and add one each week.
Before an important presentation, ask a colleague to find the weakest claim in your material. Strengthen it or cut it.
low: Before you prepare, write down the three things you are least certain about in your material. Check each one.
Replace any figure or example more than a year old with something current. A stale number tells the audience you have stopped paying attention.
Where a gap remains, say so, and say when you will close it: "I do not know yet. I will have the answer by Thursday."
Answer the question every expert faces: how much detail should I share? Decide it for this audience, and write the answer at the top of your notes.
Explain your hardest idea to someone outside your field. Where they lose you, add an example.

practise.high: Refresh one example in a presentation you give often. Replace it with something from the last three months.
practise.low: Before you prepare, write down the three things you are least certain about in your material. Check each one.

note.text: Expertise has no value to an audience that does not understand.

Understands their subject.deeper: Chapter Two. Workbook Tool 12: The Knowledge Ladder.

online.title: The best way to explain complex concepts, Part 2

Defines the presentation objective.name: Defines the presentation objective
Defines the presentation objective.measures: Whether you know, before you prepare, what the audience should know, understand and do when you finish, and whether you can say your core message in one sentence.

score.high: You start at the end. You know what you want from the audience before you build anything. That is the single most useful preparation habit there is.
score.low: This is a high-return place to start. When the objective is unclear, the presentation grows to fill the gap. Deciding the outcome first will make everything after it shorter and sharper.

Defines the presentation objective.matters: An audience can only act on what they understand. If you cannot say what you want from them, they cannot give it to you. A clear objective also tells you what to cut.

high: Test your single sentence on a colleague before you prepare. Ask them to say it back. Use their words if they are better than yours.
Check your verb. If your objective says "share" or "outline", ask whether you mean "convince" or "persuade". Change the verb and everything changes.
Use the objective as your editor. Before you add any slide or story, ask whether it moves the audience towards that sentence.
Write down what the audience should be able to tell other people afterwards. If they could not repeat it, sharpen it.
Decide how you will know it worked: a decision taken, a budget agreed, a next meeting booked. Write it down before you present.
low: Complete this sentence before anything else: "After this presentation, the audience will..." Keep going until someone else could judge whether you succeeded.
Choose your verb. Explaining, persuading and justifying each need different words, different evidence and a different close. Pick one.
Decide how big a change you are asking for: "you could do this better", "you need to fix this", or "this cannot go on". Each one needs a different case.
Write down what you want the audience to know, to feel and to do when you finish. One line for each.
Write the last line of your presentation first: the action you will ask for. Build everything towards it.

practise.high: Test your single sentence on a colleague before you prepare. Ask them to say it back. Use their words if they are better than yours.
practise.low: Complete this sentence before anything else: "After this presentation, the audience will..." Keep going until someone else could judge whether you succeeded.

note.text: There is no such thing as "I am only presenting data". Your data does have meaning.

Defines the presentation objective.deeper: Chapter Three. Workbook Tool 2: Statement of Intent.

online.title: The one thing that will make you a better communicator

Identifies the key points.name: Identifies the key points
Identifies the key points.measures: How well you choose what to include: the few points that matter most to this audience, the evidence behind each, and the discipline to leave out what you know but they do not need.

score.high: You edit hard. You choose a few points, back each one with evidence, and resist the urge to say everything you know.
score.low: Your opportunity is in the cut. You may include too much because every piece feels important to you. Choosing fewer points will make each one land harder.

Identifies the key points.matters: An audience can carry three points out of a meeting, rarely more. Give them ten and they choose for themselves, and they may choose the wrong three. Evidence turns a point into an argument: one strong number or one real example is enough.

high: For each key point, find the one piece of evidence that makes it hard to argue with.
Find the strongest objection to your case and answer it before anyone asks.
Put every point through the "so what?" test. The more senior and busy the audience, the faster they will ask it.
Find the one point the audience must never forget, and give it the most time, the best example and the last word.
Test every slide and story against your single sentence. Anything that does not move the audience towards it goes.
low: Write down everything you could say. Cut it to the three points that matter most to this audience.
Check each point against your single sentence. If it does not support it, it goes, however much work went into it.
Ask what you would say if you had two minutes. That is the essence. Build out from there.
Decide who each piece of detail is for. If it serves you more than the audience, move it to a note they can read afterwards.
Boil the presentation down to its essence, the way a cook reduces a sauce: shorter and stronger, with none of the flavour lost. Then say it aloud in under a minute.

practise.high: For each key point, find the one piece of evidence that makes it hard to argue with.
practise.low: Write down everything you could say. Cut it to the three points that matter most to this audience.

note.text: If you cannot explain what you want to say in a single sentence, you do not know.

Identifies the key points.deeper: Chapter Three. Workbook Tool 3: The Central Argument, and Tool 6: Clutter Audit.

online.title: The small changes to your speech that will have a big effect

Organises content into a clear structure.name: Organises content into a clear structure
Organises content into a clear structure.measures: Whether your presentation has a beginning, a middle and an end the audience can follow; whether the opening tells them why it matters; and whether the close gives them a clear next step.

score.high: Your audiences can follow you. You open with a purpose, you build in a clear order, and you finish with a next step. That structure lets your content do its work.
score.low: This is one of the fastest places to improve. A simple three-act structure, used every time, will make your presentations easier to follow straight away.

Organises content into a clear structure.matters: Audiences remember beginnings and endings best. The middle needs signposts so they know where they are. A clear structure frees the audience to think about your argument.

high: Give each act a headline: a full sentence that makes a claim. Read the three headlines in order. They should make your argument on their own.
Turn your story into a question, and judge every slide by whether it helps answer it.
Match the structure to the job. With bad news, people usually know it already. Spend Act One on what happens next.
Take questions before your close, then finish with the line you prepared. The last word should be yours.
Use a template for the job in hand: a progress report, a recommendation, a product sale, a decision, training or bad news. Each one opens differently.
low: Build your next presentation in three acts. Act One: why this matters to them. Act Two: the case, in two or three points. Act Three: what happens next.
Write the first and last sixty seconds word for word, and rehearse them until they are certain.
Build the bridge into Act Two: describe what happens if they do nothing. It gives the middle a reason to exist.
Open with the audience's situation. Your own background can wait until Act Two, if it is needed at all.
Signpost the middle. Tell the audience how many points there are, and say when you move from one to the next.

practise.high: Give each act a headline: a full sentence that makes a claim. Read the three headlines in order. They should make your argument on their own.
practise.low: Build your next presentation in three acts. Act One: why this matters to them. Act Two: the case, in two or three points. Act Three: what happens next.

note.text: The purpose of the beginning is to get people ready for the middle.

Organises content into a clear structure.deeper: Chapter Three. Workbook Tool 4: The Three-Act Storyboard, and Tool 8: Prologue and Epilogue.

online.title: Even the shortest story needs structure

Tests and refines the draft.name: Tests and refines the draft
Tests and refines the draft.measures: Whether you try your draft on other people before you present, and whether you are willing to change it when they show you something.

score.high: You test before you deliver, and you act on what you hear. That habit catches problems while they are still cheap to fix.
score.low: You have an easy gain here. A ten-minute conversation about your draft will save hours of rebuilding and show you how the audience will hear it.

Tests and refines the draft.matters: You know what you mean. The audience only knows what you say. Testing the story out loud shows you the gap between the two. When people play your story back, the words they use are often your best headlines and soundbites.

high: Test your story on two people: one who knows the subject and one who does not. Listen hardest to the second.
Write down the words they use when they play it back, and use the best of them.
Show the story to key stakeholders before the day. It works as market testing, and it turns critics into co-authors.
When feedback is good, ask why it worked. Then you can repeat it on purpose.
Hold a short review after every important presentation: one thing to keep, one thing to change. Write both into your next draft.
low: Before you build any slides, run the first two minutes out loud to a trusted colleague. Ask one question: "What is the one thing I should change?" Then change it.
Edit your script for repetition, pretension and jargon. Then say it out loud. If you wince, rewrite it.
Ask whether the most senior person in the room could repeat back, in their own words, why your proposal is worth the money. If the answer is no, test it again.
Test the draft on someone who knows little about your subject. Where they look lost, the audience will be lost too.
Ask "so what?" after every claim in your draft. If you cannot answer it in a sentence, fix the claim or cut it.

practise.high: Test your story on two people: one who knows the subject and one who does not. Listen hardest to the second.
practise.low: Before you build any slides, run the first two minutes out loud to a trusted colleague. Ask one question: "What is the one thing I should change?" Then change it.

note.text: An hour spent agreeing the message saves many hours of rework on slides.

Tests and refines the draft.deeper: Chapter Three. Workbook Tool 5: The Soundbite.

Creates effective support materials.name: Creates effective support materials
Creates effective support materials.measures: How well your slides, handouts, props and activities help the audience understand and remember your points.

score.high: Your visuals support your message. Your slides are clean, and you use other materials when they help the audience understand.
score.low: Your opportunity is to make your slides work harder with less on them. A few simple changes will bring the audience's eyes back to you.

Creates effective support materials.matters: A slide that repeats your words adds nothing, and the audience reads it faster than you speak it. A slide that shows what words cannot, a picture, a single number, a comparison, makes the point stick. Every slide that does not serve the argument weakens it.

high: Replace one slide of bullet points with a single image or a single statement. Notice how the room responds.
Reveal points one at a time. A slide that shows everything at once makes the audience choose between reading and listening.
Use the visual for emphasis and your voice for explanation. Audiences believe their eyes over their ears.
When the slide changes, look at the room and say nothing for a moment while they take it in. Then speak.
Design for the back row. If a number or label cannot be read from there, make it bigger or take it out.
low: Go through your next deck slide by slide. Ask of each one: does this illustrate my point, or repeat it? Cut or change every slide that repeats.
Write your story before you open the slide software.
Introduce each complex slide with the why. Explain it in as little detail as the audience needs. Summarise it and move on.
Give each slide one idea. If a slide needs a second idea, it needs a second slide.
Ask whether you need slides at all. For a short talk or a small room, one handout or a flip chart may serve the audience better.

practise.high: Replace one slide of bullet points with a single image or a single statement. Notice how the room responds.
practise.low: Go through your next deck slide by slide. Ask of each one: does this illustrate my point, or repeat it? Cut or change every slide that repeats.

note.text: If your slides are good, say as little as you can in support of the visuals.

Creates effective support materials.deeper: Chapter Four, Section One. Workbook Tool 7: Visual Aid Review.

online.title: The simple rules that help us design better visual aids, Part Two

Uses interesting and powerful language.name: Uses interesting and powerful language
Uses interesting and powerful language.measures: Whether your words make the point stick: memorable phrases, striking facts and quotes, and plain language free of jargon the audience may not share.

score.high: Your language does work. You choose words people can repeat, you use facts that change how people see things, and you keep jargon out.
score.low: This is a quick win. Your content may be sound and still sound functional. A few deliberate choices of words will make it stay with people long after the meeting.

Uses interesting and powerful language.matters: A message sticks when people can recall it, repeat it and feel it. Functional language passes through the audience. One sharp phrase, one fact with a frame around it, one comparison they already understand, will travel out of the room and be repeated to people who were never there.

high: Listen for your soundbite as you test the story out loud. It is usually in the words other people use when they play your story back.
Find the metaphor in the words the audience uses about itself, and build on it.
Replace every "hopefully" with "if... then". Audiences respond to certainty.
Use rhythm. Group your strongest ideas in threes, and give the third the most weight.
Test any quotation against three questions: is it relevant, does it resonate, can people repeat it? If it fails one, leave it out.
low: Take your key message and write it in plain English. Read it aloud. If you would never say it in conversation, rewrite it.
Hunt the abstract nouns. Swap each one for the concrete thing it stands for. If you mean a telephone, say "telephone".
Add one striking fact and say what it is equal to: "that is the same as..."
Cut the jargon your audience does not share. Read your script as one of them would, and circle every word they would not use.
Use certain words where you can stand behind them. Swap "we hope to" for "we will", and "might help" for "helps".

practise.high: Listen for your soundbite as you test the story out loud. It is usually in the words other people use when they play your story back.
practise.low: Take your key message and write it in plain English. Read it aloud. If you would never say it in conversation, rewrite it.

note.text: Abstraction is the curse of the business presentation.

Uses interesting and powerful language.deeper: Chapter Four, Section One. Workbook Tool 5: The Soundbite.

online.title: Inspire your audience with these proven verbal hacks

Engages the audience actively.name: Engages the audience actively
Engages the audience actively.measures: Whether you use stories and real examples to carry your key messages, and whether you plan moments for the audience to take part.

score.high: You bring your points to life with real examples and you give the audience a part to play. People remember your presentations because they took part in them.
score.low: Your opportunity is human interest. One real story, told well, will do more for your message than any amount of detail.

Engages the audience actively.matters: People remember stories. A business story is simply an account of something real that happened, with a beginning, a middle and an end. It makes an abstract argument concrete. A moment of participation, even a show of hands, turns listeners into people who are involved.

high: Find the metaphor already in the room: the image your audience uses for their own situation. Build your story around it.
Check in at each act break: did I get this right, and is there anything you would add?
Never ask a question and then tell people the right answer. Use what they give you.
Online, plan an interaction every few minutes. Dead time is death to a webinar.
Collect one real example from the audience during the session and use it in your close.
low: Find one real example from your own experience that shows your central point. Tell it as a beginning, a middle and an end, in under two minutes.
Open with one question: "Of all the things we will cover today, which matters most to you?" Then use the answers.
Give people time to think before you ask for answers. A minute to make a note gets far better replies than calling on someone cold.
Start with questions people can answer easily: a show of hands, a quick vote, a one-word reply. Move to open questions once the room is warm.
Send the audience away and bring them back: a short task in pairs, then back to you. It resets attention.

practise.high: Find the metaphor already in the room: the image your audience uses for their own situation. Build your story around it.
practise.low: Find one real example from your own experience that shows your central point. Tell it as a beginning, a middle and an end, in under two minutes.

note.text: Even a short presentation can feel like being force-fed porridge if the audience is not given time to breathe.

Engages the audience actively.deeper: Chapter Four, Section One. Workbook Tool 4: The Three-Act Storyboard.

online.title: Make your sales presentations land and stick, using ancient stories

Handles questions effectively.name: Handles questions effectively
Handles questions effectively.measures: How well you prepare for questions, leave time for them, admit what you do not know, and keep control when someone tries to take over.

score.high: You treat questions as part of the presentation. You prepare for them, you answer them well, and you stay in charge of the room.
score.low: This is an opportunity to turn the riskiest part of a presentation into one of its strongest. Most of the work happens before you stand up.

Handles questions effectively.matters: Questions are where the audience tests whether you mean it. A clear, calm answer, including "I do not know, and I will find out", builds more trust than the presentation itself. A session that one person takes over leaves everyone else unheard.

high: Prepare for the hardest question, the one you hope nobody asks.
Prepare each answer three ways: in fifteen seconds, in two minutes and in ten. Use the shortest unless the room asks for more.
Meet a hostile question in four steps: acknowledge the concern, thank them for raising it, agree with what you can, then give your answer.
On a panel, keep each answer to three sentences at most. If the audience wants more, they will ask.
Prepare for the five questions every audience carries: how is this useful to me, what do I need to do, what is the risk, where is the evidence, and what will it cost?
low: Write down ten questions you might be asked and prepare a clear answer to each.
Take questions after each act and before your close, so the last word is yours.
Repeat each question before you answer it, and check that it is a question. Practise saying "I do not know, and I will find out" until it sounds confident.
Wait three seconds after the question ends before you answer. It shows you listened, and it gives you time to think.
Predict questions from the material you cut. The audience will often ask about exactly what you left out.

practise.high: Prepare for the hardest question, the one you hope nobody asks.
practise.low: Write down ten questions you might be asked and prepare a clear answer to each.

note.text: Fluency is the love-child of practice and preparation.

Handles questions effectively.deeper: Chapter Five. Workbook Tool 9: The Thirty-Minute Slot Planner.

online.title: How to prepare for the unexpected questions

Rehearses to build confidence and fluenc.name: Rehearses to build confidence and fluency
Rehearses to build confidence and fluenc.measures: Whether you rehearse out loud before you present, run to time, and can leave your plan when the room needs you to.

score.high: You rehearse, you keep to time, and you know the material well enough to adapt it on the day. That is what lets you look relaxed.
score.low: This is one of the most reliable gains in the report. Rehearsal out loud turns a good presentation on paper into a confident one in the room.

Rehearses to build confidence and fluenc.matters: Reading notes and speaking are different skills, and the audience only sees one of them. When you have rehearsed, you can watch the audience. Running over time tells the room you did not prepare; finishing on time tells them you respect theirs.

high: Cut your presentation to half the time and deliver it out loud. You will find out what matters, and you will be ready when the slot shrinks.
Rehearse your answers as well as your talk. Ask a colleague to put your three hardest questions to you.
Make rehearsal harder than the day: less time, a tougher listener, no slides. Then the real thing feels easy.
Rehearse in pieces: the opening, each act, the close and your answers, until each part works on its own.
Rehearse how you say it as well as what you say. Mark where you will pause, slow down or move.
low: Rehearse out loud, standing up, six times before your next important presentation. Time each run.
Speak from short bullet points in your own words. Memorised scripts are what make people freeze.
Learn the first and last minute until they are certain. Five minutes before you start, run them once more under your breath.
Rehearse in the room if you can, or in one like it. Stand where you will stand and look where you will look.
Rehearse once with your slides and once without them. When you can do it without them, the slides support you and stop being a script.

practise.high: Cut your presentation to half the time and deliver it out loud. You will find out what matters, and you will be ready when the slot shrinks.
practise.low: Rehearse out loud, standing up, six times before your next important presentation. Time each run.

note.text: Write much less and rehearse much more.

Rehearses to build confidence and fluenc.deeper: Chapter Five. Workbook Tool 8: Prologue and Epilogue, and Tool 9: The Thirty-Minute Slot Planner.

online.title: 5 really simple and cheap ways to improve your presentation skills

Uses voice with skill.name: Uses voice with skill
Uses voice with skill.measures: How well you use your voice: clear speech, the pause, changes of pace, emphasis on key words, the right volume, and adjusting for people listening in a second language.

score.high: Your voice carries your message. You use pace, emphasis and the pause to help the audience hear what matters.
score.low: Your opportunity is to bring your conversational voice into the room. In ordinary conversation you already use your full range. Under pressure, you narrow it. A little practice brings it back.

Uses voice with skill.matters: The voice tells the audience which words matter. A pause after your key point gives the idea time to land, and it feels far longer to you than to them. A steady, even voice asks the audience to do the work of finding your point. Clear articulation matters more than speed, above all for people listening in a second language. Finish your consonants and the pace looks after itself.

high: Mark the three sentences that matter most and leave three seconds of silence after each.
In each key sentence, underline the one word that carries the meaning and give it a little more weight.
Speak to the end of the line. Keep your energy through the last word of each sentence, where the point usually sits.
When English is not your audience's first language, slow your key sentences and finish every consonant. Being understood is your job.
Vary your pace on purpose: slower for the point that matters, a little faster for the story that leads to it.
low: Read a page of a book aloud: breathe at each comma, pause twice as long at each full stop and three times as long at a new paragraph. Five minutes a day for a week.
Finish every word, above all the last consonant. Say the hard sounds properly and your speed looks after itself.
Record yourself rehearsing and listen back for the flat stretches. Mark them, and rehearse those sections again.
Speak with your own voice: the one you use with a friend across the table, with the volume turned up for the room.
Find your energy setting. Picture a dial from nought to ten. Nervous speakers sit at about three. Aim for six or seven.

practise.high: Mark the three sentences that matter most and leave three seconds of silence after each.
practise.low: Read a page of a book aloud: breathe at each comma, pause twice as long at each full stop and three times as long at a new paragraph. Five minutes a day for a week.

note.text: Pause for breath where there is a comma. Pause for the audience to breathe where there is a full stop.

Uses body language with purpose.name: Uses body language with purpose
Uses body language with purpose.measures: How you use movement, gesture, position, eye contact and expression to support what you are saying.

score.high: Your body supports your words. You move with purpose, you hold eye contact, and the audience reads the same message from you as they hear.
score.low: This is an area where small, specific changes make a visible difference. Your nervous habits are invisible to you, and easy to fix once you know they are there.

Uses body language with purpose.matters: An audience watches before it listens. When your body and your words say the same thing, the audience trusts both. Real eye contact, a full thought with one person before moving to the next, makes each person feel spoken to.

high: Plan where you will stand for each act and when you will move. Use movement to mark a change of section.
Give each important line to one person, as if you wrote it for them.
When nerves narrow your range, broaden it on purpose: a bigger gesture, a fuller expression, a longer look.
Use your face. Try saying "no" with your eyebrows down and then up, and notice how the meaning changes.
Look at the audience as you speak, and say nothing while you look to your notes for the next cue.
low: Ask a colleague to watch your next presentation for one thing only: habits such as swaying, hands in pockets or a closed stance.
Finish each sentence with one person. Give them the whole thought before you move to the next.
When you look down at your notes or turn to the screen, stop speaking. Look up, then speak.
Plant your feet for your opening line. Stand still while you say it, then move.
Watch a recording of yourself with the sound off. Find the one habit that distracts most, and fix that first.

practise.high: Plan where you will stand for each act and when you will move. Use movement to mark a change of section.
practise.low: Ask a colleague to watch your next presentation for one thing only: habits such as swaying, hands in pockets or a closed stance.

note.text: Face the audience and make simple eye contact with them. That is all that matters.

Manages psychological and emotional stat.name: Manages psychological and emotional state
Manages psychological and emotional stat.measures: How you manage nerves before and during a presentation, whether your attention is on the audience or on yourself, and how you read and respond to the room as you go.

score.high: You manage your nerves and keep your attention on the audience. You read the room and adjust as you go. That is presence.
score.low: Your opportunity is to move your attention from yourself to the audience. Nerves are normal, and you can learn to use them.

Manages psychological and emotional stat.matters: Nerves bring energy, and the energy is useful. The trouble starts when your attention turns inward: nervousness is almost always a symptom of self-focus. When you wonder whether you are doing it right, you are nervous. When you wonder whether the audience understands, you are busy. An audience relaxes when you do, and engages when you are clearly watching them.

high: Watch the audience in the first two minutes and adjust your energy to what you see.
Prepare one line for the moment something goes wrong, so you can smile, say it and move on.
Keep a record of presentations that went well, and read it before the next big one. Confidence comes from technique and experience multiplied.
Build a best-moment routine: recall your best presentation with all five senses, add a word, then a small gesture. Use it before you go on.
Plan your recovery from the thing you fear most: what you will do, where you will walk and the line you will say.
low: Build a short routine for the ten minutes before you present: breathing, a little movement, a moment of quiet. Use it every time.
Write down the three things you want the audience to take away, and hold your attention there. When your mind turns to how you feel, look at the audience.
If something goes wrong, do not apologise. Smile, and carry on. An audience will forgive almost anything unless you embarrass them.
Decide who you are talking to in your head. Picture one friendly person in the room, and talk to them.
If you feel underprepared, you probably are. Book one extra rehearsal into your diary before the day.

practise.high: Watch the audience in the first two minutes and adjust your energy to what you see.
practise.low: Build a short routine for the ten minutes before you present: breathing, a little movement, a moment of quiet. Use it every time.

note.text: Most people prepare the content and forget to prepare the person.

online.title: This is what every nervous speaker needs to be told

plan.text: Ninety days is long enough to turn a new habit into the way you work. It is short enough to keep your attention. The plan has three stages. Each one asks you to practise one thing in real presentations, then check what difference it made.
[What to practise next, from the Priority 1 page, in the reader's band.]
Use it in at least two real presentations this month. After each one, ask: what difference did the change make to me, and my audience? Write the answer down in one line.
[What to practise next, from the Priority 2 page, in the reader's band.]
Keep the first habit going. Add the second one to at least two more presentations. Ask a colleague to watch one of them and tell you what they noticed.

Choose one presentation that matters, the kind you would normally worry about. Prepare it with both habits from the start. Rehearse it out loud. After it, read your two one-line notes from the first two months and compare.

Take the free assessment again at fff-assessment.themessagebusiness.com. Compare your two priority scores with today's: [Priority 1 score] and [Priority 2 score]. The numbers will tell you how far the habits have moved. Your audiences will already have told you.
